**Repository:** <https://github.com/Keshav-kh/CMPSC448-project1>. All numbers in this report are generated by `src/make_report.py` from the JSON files in `results/`; nothing is typed by hand.

# 1. Problem definition and dataset curation

**Task.** Given a response written by a large language model, predict which *LLM family* produced it. This is a 5-way text classification problem. We also ask whether the user prompt helps (RQ2), whether the learned "fingerprint" transfers across task types (RQ3), and which stylistic signals separate the families (RQ4).

**Source.** We use the public **UltraFeedback** dataset (`openbmb/UltraFeedback`, MIT licence; Cui et al., 2023). Each record has a prompt (`instruction`), the sub-dataset it came from (`source`: Evol-Instruct, ShareGPT, UltraChat, FLAN, TruthfulQA, FalseQA), and four completions, each tagged with the generating `model`. This gives the required (LLM_name, LLM_input, LLM_output) triples directly. The raw files contain {raw_completions} completions for {raw_prompts} unique prompts from 17 models. Because every prompt was answered by four randomly chosen models, **the same prompt appears with several different labels**, which matters for RQ2. No private data is involved; we did not query any model ourselves.

**Family grouping.** We grouped models by developer and kept only unambiguous ones:

| family | models |
|---|---|
| GPT (OpenAI) | gpt-3.5-turbo, gpt-4 |
| LLaMA-2 (Meta) | llama-2-7b-chat, llama-2-13b-chat, llama-2-70b-chat |
| Bard (Google, predecessor of Gemini) | bard |
| Falcon (TII) | falcon-40b-instruct |
| MPT (MosaicML) | mpt-30b-chat |

We dropped third-party LLaMA fine-tunes (Vicuna, WizardLM, UltraLM, Alpaca): they share LLaMA's base weights but were tuned largely on GPT-distilled data, so assigning them to either family would blur the labels. We also dropped StarChat (a code-only model) and Pythia-12B (only 834 completions).

**Cleaning and balancing.** Starting from {after_family_filter} completions of the kept models, we removed empty texts, exact duplicate responses and duplicate (prompt, model) pairs, and kept responses of 10–1000 words. {after_length_filter} rows remained, but they were very unbalanced (LLaMA-2 {llama_before} vs Bard {bard_before}). We randomly downsampled every family to 4,000 rows, giving **{n_total} examples** and {n_unique_prompts} unique prompts.

**Task label.** For RQ3 we derived a task label for every prompt. TruthfulQA and FalseQA prompts become *factual_qa*. For all others we apply keyword rules on the prompt, in order: code terms give *coding*; math terms or arithmetic give *math*; remaining FLAN prompts give *nlp_task*; writing verbs (write, essay, story, email, ...) give *writing*; everything else is *chat*.

{task_table}

**Split.** We split 80/10/10 *by unique prompt* (seed 448), so a prompt and all its responses fall in a single split. The code asserts that no prompt crosses splits. After downsampling, {prompts_with_multiple_families} prompts are still answered by more than one family.

{data_table}

# 2. Models and training

**Tokenisation.** We use a case-preserving regex tokenizer (`\n|\w+|[^\w\s]`). Every punctuation mark is its own token and newlines become a `<nl>` token, so formatting stays visible to the models. The vocabulary is built from the training split only (minimum frequency 2, capped at {vocab} entries, including `<pad>`, `<unk>` and `<sep>`). Sequences are truncated to 256 tokens. Batches are padded dynamically, and padding is masked out of every pooling operation.

**CNN.** Embedding (128-d), then three parallel `Conv1d` layers with kernel sizes 3, 4 and 5 (128 filters each, ReLU), then masked max-over-time pooling, concatenation (384-d), dropout 0.5 and a linear layer to 5 classes. {cnn_params} parameters.

**RNN (BiLSTM).** Embedding (128-d), a 1-layer bidirectional LSTM (64 hidden units per direction), then masked mean pooling and masked max pooling over time, concatenated (256-d), dropout 0.5 and a linear layer to 5 classes. {rnn_params} parameters.

**Training.** Adam (learning rate 1e-3), cross-entropy loss, batch size 64, gradient clipping at 5. Batches are bucketed by length to reduce padding. We train for at most 6 epochs with early stopping on validation accuracy (patience 2) and restore the best-validation weights before testing. Every configuration is run with seeds 1, 2 and 3, and we report mean ± standard deviation of test accuracy and macro-F1. For RQ1/RQ2 the best validation epochs were {cnn_best_epochs} (CNN) and {rnn_best_epochs} (BiLSTM).

**Hardware and run time.** All RQ1/RQ2 runs were trained on a laptop CPU (16 logical cores, PyTorch 2.9.1 CPU build), four runs in parallel with four threads each. One output-only run took {cnn_time} min (CNN) or {rnn_time} min (BiLSTM) on average. Our first BiLSTM (128 hidden units, packed sequences) needed more than 10 minutes per epoch. We therefore halved the hidden size and dropped sequence packing, which was about 3× slower on this CPU. Masked pooling keeps padding out of the representation, so packing is not needed for correctness. Every result file records the device it ran on.

**Baselines.** (a) TF-IDF over word unigrams and bigrams (case-preserving, punctuation kept, sublinear tf), followed by logistic regression (C = 4). (b) A gradient-boosting classifier on 34 hand-crafted style features (RQ4).

# 3. Results

## RQ1: Can we identify which LLM generated a response?

Output-only classification on the held-out test split (1,992 responses, about 400 per family):

{rq1_table}

Both neural models are far above chance (20%). The **CNN ({cnn_acc}%) beats the BiLSTM ({rnn_acc}%)** by about six points and is also about 2.5× faster to train. The simple TF-IDF baseline is stronger still ({tfidf_out}%); Section 5 explains why.

Per-family test accuracy (recall), mean over seeds:

{rq1_family_table}

![CNN, output only: confusion matrix summed over 3 seeds (rows normalised).](figures/cm_cnn_output_none.png){{width=48%}} ![BiLSTM, output only: confusion matrix summed over 3 seeds.](figures/cm_rnn_output_none.png){{width=48%}}

**Bard** is the easiest family for every model ({cnn_fam_Bard}% with the CNN), followed by **LLaMA-2** ({cnn_fam_LLaMA-2}%). **MPT** is the hardest ({cnn_fam_MPT}% with the CNN, {rnn_fam_MPT}% with the BiLSTM). The CNN sends {mpt_to_gpt}% of MPT responses to GPT and {mpt_to_bard}% to Bard. MPT-30B-chat's fine-tuning data includes ShareGPT conversations, which are largely ChatGPT outputs, so a GPT-like style is plausible. Falcon and GPT are also often confused with each other.

## RQ2: Does the user's prompt help identify the LLM?

The same code, vocabulary procedure and hyperparameters are used for all three setups. *Input + output* is the prompt (first 64 tokens), then `<sep>`, then the response, truncated to 256 tokens in total.

{rq2_table}

![RQ2: test accuracy by input setup (error bars: std over 3 seeds).](figures/rq2_setups.png){{width=75%}}

**(i) Can the LLM be predicted from the prompt alone? Essentially no.** Input-only accuracy is {cnn_input}% (CNN), {rnn_input}% (BiLSTM) and {tfidf_input}% (TF-IDF). That is barely above uniform chance (20%) and the test majority class rate ({maj_rate}%). This is what we expected: UltraFeedback assigned models to prompts at random, so the prompt says almost nothing about who answered it. Prompts also repeat across families. {multi_rows} rows share their prompt with a response from a different family, and identical inputs with different labels cannot all be classified correctly. Even an oracle that always predicted the most common family per test prompt would be capped at {upper_bound}%.

**Is the small gain above chance real, and where does it come from?** A one-sided binomial test of the TF-IDF input-only accuracy against 20% gives p = {p_uniform}. Against the majority-class rate it gives p = {p_major}, so the model does no better than always guessing the largest class. The little signal that exists is **dataset leakage, not a property of the models**. Bard has no responses at all in three FLAN sub-sets (NIv2, P3, FLAN-2021) and is over-represented in Evol-Instruct and UltraChat, so the prompt's *source* is weakly informative. A logistic regression on the one-hot source alone reaches {meta_source}%, more than any text model. Almost all of that signal identifies Bard: TF-IDF input-only recall for Bard is {tfidf_input_bard}%, while the other families are near or below 20%. The derived task label ({meta_task}%) and prompt length ({meta_plen}%) carry no signal; median prompt lengths are {plen} words.

**(ii) Does adding the input improve classification? No. It never helps, and it hurts slightly for the BiLSTM and TF-IDF; for the CNN the difference is within seed noise.** Input + output is {cnn_both}% for the CNN vs {cnn_output}% output-only, {rnn_both}% vs {rnn_output}% for the BiLSTM, and {tfidf_both}% vs {tfidf_output}% for TF-IDF. Prepending the prompt uses up part of the fixed 256-token budget, which cuts off part of the response, and the prompt tokens themselves are mostly noise for this task.

**(iii) When could input-only work "surprisingly well"?** When the data collection links prompts to models: each model answering a different prompt pool, different system prompts, or sources with different topics. A classifier would then learn the *collection process* rather than the LLM. Our near-chance result, together with the source-only check, suggests our split is largely free of this effect. The remaining effect is small and fully explained by Bard's source distribution.

# 4. In-depth analysis

## RQ3: Do LLM fingerprints generalise across tasks?

**Setup.** For each task *T* we train the CNN (3 seeds) on the training split *without any task-T rows*, early-stop on validation rows not from *T*, and test on task-*T* rows. We compare against the in-domain CNN from RQ1, whose training data includes task *T*, *on exactly the same test rows*. As a larger second sample we also report accuracy on *all* task-*T* rows across all splits, since the held-out model never saw any of them. For *writing* and *coding* we repeat the experiment with the BiLSTM.

{rq3_table}

![Response length by family.](figures/rq4_length_box.png){{width=48%}} ![Markdown use by family.](figures/rq4_markdown.png){{width=48%}}

**Vocabulary.** We compared the 1,000 most frequent lower-cased words of each family on the training split. Overlap (Jaccard similarity) ranges from {jac_lo} to {jac_hi}. The vocabularies differ mostly in topic words and in "assistant" phrases, not in core vocabulary.

**A classifier on hand-crafted features only.** We built 34 features in five groups: length, lexical, markdown, punctuation and opening phrase (`src/features.py`). Logistic regression on these features reaches {feat_lr}% test accuracy, and histogram gradient boosting reaches **{feat_gb}%** (macro-F1 {feat_gb_f1}%). That is already better than our BiLSTM, using no word identities at all. The top permutation importances on the test set are {top_feats}.
